articles.title: Slow Oscillations Modulate Overnight Brain Changes in Working Memory Function
articles.content: Working memory (WM), the transient storage and manipulation of information, is a cognitive function that can improve with training. Accumulating evidence suggests that sleep, particularly slow oscillations (SOs) that occur during nonrapid eye movement sleep, supports this improvement. Yet, how sleep and SOs in particular relate to neural processes supporting WM remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how WM-related neural activity evolves across nocturnal sleep and how these changes relate to neural processing during SOs. Participants performed a WM task during fMRI before and after sleep, with simultaneous EEG–fMRI capturing neural activity during the first 2.5 hr of sleep. Our results showed significant overnight changes in WM-related activity, characterized by reduced recruitment of the dorsal precuneus during WM encoding/maintenance phases and frontal regions during the retrieval phase of WM. In addition, sleep increased item-specific reinstatement in a sensory processing region during WM. This pattern of results suggests a combined influence of sleep on enhancing sensory reinstatement while reducing potential top–down control (i.e., reduced parietal and frontal activity). Critically, SO-related activity was directly linked to overnight activity changes: Stronger SO activation in the premotor cortex and ventromedial pFC predicted greater overnight reductions in WM-related activity, and multivoxel analyses in the ventral attention network revealed a parallel relationship. These findings suggest that SOs play a critical role in WM function by facilitating the reorganization of WM-related processing.

articles.title: Transformer Mechanisms Mimic Frontostriatal Gating Operations When Trained on Human Working Memory Tasks
articles.content: Working memory (WM) is thought to rely on sophisticated frontostriatal mechanisms for selective gating, supporting updating and readout of information to and from distinct memory “addresses” (neural populations). According to computational models, capacity limitations in WM arise due to challenges in “role addressability”: learning to correctly bind items in memory to their respective roles and assigning credit to the corresponding gating operations. However, these conclusions are based on particular assumptions about biological neural networks, and it is unclear whether the principles generalize to other architectures. To address this question, we examine whether similar gating mechanisms emerge in Transformer neural network architectures, which have demonstrated success on tasks requiring executive function—the ability to represent, coordinate, and manage multiple subtasks—yet lack intentionally built-in gating mechanisms. We analyze the mechanisms that emerge within Transformers trained on human WM tasks explicitly designed to place demands on gating. We find that the Transformer's attention mechanism develops role-addressable input and output gating, but only when trained on task distributions that benefit from frontostriatal-like gating mechanisms. Moreover, these gating strategies support enhanced generalization and variable binding and increase the models' effective capacity to store and access multiple items in memory, resembling the constraints found in frontostriatal models. These results suggest that gating mechanisms serve a fundamental computational role in managing role addressability and binding and highlight opportunities for future research on computational similarities between modern artificial intelligence architectures and models of the human brain.

articles.title: Visual Perspective Shapes Subjective Experience: Dissociable Parietal Contributions to the Constructive Nature of Memory
articles.content: Subjective features of memory are often treated as secondary to the objective content of remembered events. However, growing evidence suggests that these features actively shape how memories are constructed, experienced, and used. Rather than treating visual perspective as a peripheral correlate of subjectivity, this review positions it as a key mechanism that shapes the memory. Because perspective can be flexibly controlled and reliably measured, it offers a unique window into how retrieval goals interact with mental simulation to produce vivid and emotionally resonant recollections. Drawing on behavioral and neuroimaging research, this review shows that visual perspective determines the spatial framing of memory and the emotional and sensory qualities of recollection. Focusing on the posterior parietal cortex, it outlines distinct roles for the angular gyrus (AG) and the precuneus in supporting perspective-dependent retrieval. The AG contributes to the selection and maintenance of a retrieval perspective, integrating perceptual and conceptual features into a coherent scene. In contrast, the precuneus supports spatial transformation and modulates the vividness, emotional tone, and embodied character of recollection, particularly when individuals recall events from a nondominant or shifted perspective. Together, these findings position visual perspective as a central mechanism in the construction of subjectivity. Understanding how perspective shapes the process of remembering provides insight into how memory supports emotion regulation, mental simulation, and the continuity of the self across time.

articles.title: Memory Traces Reflect How They Were Last Accessed
articles.content: Episodic memories are known to change with each act of retrieval. We hypothesize that accessing semantic knowledge in different ways during episodic retrieval—from unique perceptual features to taxonomic and thematic context—shapes how those memories are subsequently represented during recognition. In this fMRI study, human participants learned novel word–image pairs and underwent re-exposure that required accessing semantic knowledge at one of three different levels: item, category, or theme. Participants then completed a recognition task. Although behavioral memory performance was matched across conditions, neural activity during recognition varied based on prior semantic access history. Recognition patterns could be classified according to prior semantic access in early visual cortex, ventral temporal cortex, and the hippocampus for remembered concepts. A whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed bilateral clusters along the ventral visual stream where semantic access history was decodable. To further characterize how prior semantic access history shaped neural representations during recognition, we tested whether memories accessed at the same semantic level were expressed more similarly or distinctly in the brain. Category-level access increased similarity among items in early visual cortex, whereas item-level access led to more differentiated representations in the visual word form area. Together, these findings show that how we access semantic knowledge during episodic retrieval leaves measurable traces in subsequent neural representations, revealing how semantic–episodic interactions shape memory representations.

articles.title: The Temporal Dynamics of Attentional Allocation during Counterfactual Learning
articles.content: Counterfactual learning, the ability to learn from what could have happened under different circumstances, is a key cognitive mechanism supporting behavioral adaptation. While its neural and computational underpinnings are increasingly understood, the temporal dynamics of attention toward factual and counterfactual outcomes remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigate the biological mechanisms underlying this process using a reinforcement learning task combined with eye-tracking and pupillometry in 36 human participants. Participants completed a two-armed bandit task with full outcome feedback and exhibited a robust confirmation bias, learning more from outcomes that supported their previous choices. Gaze patterns revealed a consistent temporal sequence of fixations from factual to counterfactual outcomes, modulated in opposite directions by the valence of each outcome. Pupil dilation, a proxy for noradrenergic arousal, was influenced by the factual outcome and by the similarity between factual and counterfactual feedback, consistent with increased surprise during disconfirmatory events. These results provide a mechanistic account of how attentional and arousal systems jointly shape outcome evaluation. By integrating behavioral modeling with physiological markers, this work contributes to a broader understanding of the adaptive constraints on decision-making and offers new insight into how organisms evaluate hypothetical alternatives in learning contexts.

articles.title: Theta and High-alpha Phase-locking Dynamics Unveil Face Perception in Ambiguous Stimuli
articles.content: Previous studies emphasize phase synchronization as a fundamental mechanism for integrating local features into coherent percepts. We employed a novel paradigm and dynamic graph analysis based on EEG to track neural dynamics associated with perceiving a face (or not) while keeping the stimuli identical. Thirty participants underwent a pretest to establish perceptual thresholds for detecting faces within images overlaid with visual noise. These thresholds were then applied in an EEG experiment with the same task, focusing on images with 50% and 75% detection probabilities. In the high-alpha band, we observed increased coupling (100–275 msec after stimulus onset) between the left and right occipitotemporal electrodes when an ambiguous stimulus was perceived as a face, indicating conscious face perception. The failure to perceive a face resulted in enhanced theta band phase synchronization between bilateral occipitotemporal electrodes and increased high-alpha-band coupling between the left frontal and right occipitotemporal electrodes, which showed face-selective responses. These synchronizations are likely to reflect the continuous gathering of individual bits of facial information rather than signaling the presence or absence of a face percept. Additionally, we identified frontal–occipitotemporal theta-band couplings related to the stimulus’s informational content, irrespective of whether the inherent face was perceived. Our findings reveal distinct temporal dynamics in phase synchronization at specific frequencies, indicating a specialized system for face perception during integrated information processing across the frontal and visual cortex, resolving ambiguities.

articles.title: Capturing the Attentional Trade-off between Speech Planning and Comprehension
articles.content: In conversation, future speakers often plan speech simultaneously with comprehension, which means that they must divide attentional resources between these processes. In this EEG study, we used responses to linguistic attention probes (i.e., syllable “BA” presented during spoken sentences) to track temporal variations in attention to comprehension. Participants were asked to listen to prerecorded sentences with expected or unexpected sentence-final words. Each sentence was presented twice, once with and once without the attention probe starting 100 msec after the target word onset. Participants saw a picture 50 msec before the target word. Depending on the test block (picture naming or button press), participants either named the picture or pressed the space bar, both after an 850-msec delay. The probes elicited a negative potential approximately 100 msec after probe onset (i.e., an attention probe effect) in all probe conditions. Unexpectedly, neither word expectancy nor speech planning influenced the timing or strength of the attention probe effect. This indicates that expectancy of words in Dutch does not affect the allocation of attention toward these words 100 msec after their onset (i.e., the time of the probe presentation). Interestingly, engaging in speech planning does not seem to divert attentional resources away from comprehension at the moment of probe presentation. These findings imply that listeners are able to effectively distribute their attentional resources between comprehension and speech planning and carry out these processes at the same time. Considering these unexpected findings, using attention probes might not be the best approach to capture variations in temporal attention in dual-task paradigms.

articles.title: Supporting Researcher Control in AI-Assisted Social Media Analysis: A Mixed-Methods Study of AI4OSN
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.22006v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: High-quality annotated datasets are critical for advancing computational social science (CSS) research, yet collecting, curating, and analyzing large-scale data from dynamic sources such as online social networks (OSNs) remains a persistent bottleneck. Researchers must also translate substantive questions into queries, relevance criteria, and defensible interpretations. Large language models (LLMs) can assist, but they can also obscure the judgments, potentially reducing researcher oversight and critical evaluation. We present AI4OSN, a mixed-initiative platform that keeps researchers in control of data collection, relevance labeling, and sensemaking while making AI assistance available as an inspectable advisory resource. In a systematic user study (N=18) using X/Twitter data, participants reported above-benchmark perceived usability (mean SUS score of 79.7), increased confidence in LLM-assisted annotation and analysis tasks, and low cognitive workload during AI-supported sensemaking. Notably, novice participants showed descriptively greater alignment and higher reported agreement with AI output than experienced participants, underscoring the need to support differentiated verification practices across expertise levels. Overall, this work contributes both a human-centered system for social data analysis and empirical insights into how AI-assisted interfaces shape researcher behavior, trust, and decision-making. Our findings highlight design opportunities and tensions in building accessible, transparent, and agentic AI systems for social media and web research.
articles.author: Qile Wang, Abhishek Karwankar, Shukria Muhammadi, Srikanth Kumar Perumalla, Abhin Suresh, Sunita Chandrasekaran, Kenneth E. Barner, Matthew Louis Mauriello

articles.title: Synchrony, Affect, and Perceived Autonomy in Virtual Robot-Facilitated Anxiety Support Groups
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.21977v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Socially assistive robots could expand access to group-based mental health support when skilled human facilitators are unavailable. However, their effectiveness will depend on whether they foster productive interactions among participants. We examined dyadic head-movement synchrony among 96 participants across 18 virtual robot-facilitated anxiety support group sessions. A human-controlled virtual robot, via a Wizard-of-Oz (WoZ) system, facilitated all sessions. We found that stronger peak synchrony predicted lower post-session negative affect. In contrast, speakers who more often followed listeners' movements reported higher negative affect and state anxiety, demonstrating that synchrony strength and direction capture distinct interpersonal processes. Participants who believed the robot was autonomous showed more genuine synchrony and stronger peaks than those who believed it was human-operated; more negative attitudes toward robots also predicted greater synchrony. These findings support synchrony as an objective, behaviorally grounded measure for evaluating robot-facilitated groups and a potential signal for guiding future autonomous facilitators.
articles.author: A'di Dust, Mohammad Soleymani, Mina Kian, Maja Matari\'c

articles.title: It's My Turn! Interpretable Methods Reveal Developmental Differences from Mother-Child Conversational Dynamics
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.21969v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Understanding conversational interactions between mothers and children is an important challenge for computational behavioral modeling. Existing methods use traditional statistical approaches and subjective measures of conversational dynamics, without incorporating temporal or probabilistic modeling. We developed an interpretable computational framework that combines sequence analysis, information-theoretic measures, and Bayesian hierarchical modeling to characterize temporal conversational dynamics in parent-child play. We applied this framework to interactions from 94 mother-child dyads with two-year-old children. Sequence analysis revealed that dyads with lower language development (as defined by scores on the Bayley developmental test) exhibited more heterogeneous conversational organization and fewer serve-and-return exchanges than higher-development dyads, a reciprocal turn-taking pattern in which one partner initiates communication and the other responds. Mutual information analyses suggested differences in conversational predictability between lower- and higher-development dyads, although the bootstrap confidence intervals overlapped. Bayesian hierarchical models estimated temporal trajectories for maternal consecutive turns, child responses following maternal speech, and overlapping responses; HDIs showed that trajectories differed in whether they excluded 0, but there were no statistically credible differences between the Bayley groups. Overall, these results indicate that children with higher developmental scores have more organized and predictable communication styles, with more ``serve-and-return" patterns with their mothers. These results demonstrate that interpretable computational representations of conversational dynamics capture developmental differences beyond simple measures of speech quantity.
articles.author: A'di Dust, Anura Deshpande, Pat Levitt, Maja Matari\'c

articles.title: RelicTouch: Exploring Fingertip Vibrotactile Feedback for Image Interpretation
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.21642v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Vibrotactile feedback is often used to simulate material properties on interactive surfaces, but less is known about how it can help users interpret visual differences during touchscreen exploration. We present RelicTouch, a finger-worn system that converts image-derived features into movement-contingent vibration. Study 1 was a controlled within-subject experiment (n=20) examining how vibration intensity, stripe spacing, and finger configuration affected haptic--visual congruence and subjective clarity. Study 2 was an exploratory qualitative study with eight domain experts examining how users interpreted cues generated from luminance and edge variation during continuous image exploration. Results suggest that cue legibility was associated with distinguishable signal changes, movement-based comparison, and visual or task context. Single-finger exploration yielded higher subjective ratings, whereas multi-finger feedback showed possible value for coarse comparison across separated features. These findings provide initial design implications for vibrotactile image exploration beyond material-simulation-oriented rendering.
articles.author: Xiaosong Wang, Ran Liu, Yifan Feng

articles.title: Digital Qiang Garden: Artist Residency as Interface for Creativity Under Change
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.21640v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This research presents Digital Qiang Garden, an artist-led residency situated in Qiang ethnic minority villages in western Sichuan, China, as a practice-based inquiry into creativity for change. Rather than framing creativity as a discrete outcome or individual agency, the project examines how creative practice unfolds through lived conditions under uncertainty. Drawing from three years of residency practice, the pictorial identifies four creative modes of praxis that repeatedly emerged through shared living, material engagement, and cross-media collaboration. Through annotated visuals and project-based case studies, we further trace how these modes generated eight interrelated layers of change, spanning artistic processes, social relations, cultural encounters, ecological awareness, organizational structures, and artists' longer-term trajectories. By framing an artist-led residency as a transferable structure, this work contributes to HCI and creativity research by foregrounding designed conditions, situated action, and relational processes through which change unfolds over time.
articles.author: Yunyi Rainee Wang, Joshua Nijiati Alimujiang

articles.title: ClearTalk: Data-Driven Mandarin Articulation Analysis and Personalized Communication Support for Children with Dysarthria
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.21639v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Children with dysarthria may experience reduced intelligibility and difficulty expressing everyday needs. ClearTalk is a smartwatch-based system that converts Mandarin speech-recognition differences into interpretable articulatory profiles for personalized practice and staged communication. Target and recognized utterances are aligned at the syllable level, summarized across seven articulatory positions, and ranked by a count-sensitive asymmetric heuristic. For 13 dysarthric speakers from the Mandarin Dysarthria Speech Corpus, system syllable-level accuracy showed a Pearson correlation of 0.908 with expert intelligibility, with an R-squared value of 0.824 and a p-value below 0.001. The system-selected priority targets achieved an 86.7 percent overlap with the consensus of three blinded speech-language pathologists; across 210 target consonants, automated labels achieved 86.7 percent agreement, a Cohen's kappa of 0.76, and a macro-F1 score of 0.81. In a balanced single-session pilot with 15 children, mean pre/post gains were 14.4, 29.4, and 27.7 percentage points for mild, moderate, and severe groups, while communication-round completion rates were 81.3, 66.7, and 48.0 percent. These findings support the feasibility of using interpretable patterns of speech errors to guide wearable articulation practice and communication assistance.
articles.author: Ben Xiaolu Huang

articles.title: Can AI Help Explain AI? Effects of Multimodal LLM-Generated Explanations on Perceived Understanding and Perceived Trust in XAI Visualizations
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.21638v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) aims to make machine learning models understandable, yet many XAI visualizations remain difficult for end-users to interpret. Here, we evaluate whether augmenting XAI outputs with textual explanations from multimodal LLMs improves perceived understanding and perceived trust. We conducted a pre-registered within-subject experiment ($N = 128$) across seven decision scenarios and five XAI methods, with and without LLM generated explanations. The explanations improved perceived understanding and perceived trust by 0.35 and 0.26 points on five-point scales (both $p < .001$). The gain appeared in all seven scenarios, did not differ between local and global explanations, and was largest for participants with the least prior XAI exposure. A mediation analysis indicates an indirect effect on perceived trust through perceived understanding. These results suggest that multimodal LLMs can provide a useful interpretive layer for XAI beyond expert audiences.
articles.author: Mario Truss, Marc Schmitt, Stefan Feuerriegel

articles.title: Auditing Hyperstimulation at Scale in Child-Facing YouTube Videos
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.21637v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Parents, pediatricians, and journalists have raised concern that child-facing videos are becoming increasingly overstimulating, but this concern rests mostly on ad hoc observation rather than systematic measurement. We present a large-scale audit of hyperstimulation patterns, which we refer to as content-independent production choices that may exceed young children's capacity to process comfortably. Drawing on parents' Reddit discussions and developmental psychology, we identify 12 hyperstimulation patterns and operationalize them as computational metrics. We apply these metrics to 16,375 videos from 542 child-facing YouTube channels spanning 2015-2026. We found broad increases in stimulation over time, with cut rates rising across all five content categories. Nearly a quarter of the channels increased in at least one stimulation pattern over time. More stimulating videos also tended to receive more views, but the relevant stimulation patterns differed across content types.
articles.author: Shao-Yu Chu, Noel Mekogue, Qiyu Li, Xuan Liu, Shuang Hao, Haojian Jin

articles.title: Ethics Suppression in AI Development: A Comparative Case Study of Responsible AI Under Competitive Pressure
articles.content:
arXiv:2611.21629v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This study explores the governance tensions among Google, OpenAI, Meta, and Microsoft, focusing on how competitive AI development can lead to the ethics suppression. The study aims to examine how ethical oversight loses practical influence even when responsible AI structures are formally in place, especially during rapid technological competition. Despite the rapid growth of responsible AI frameworks and ethical principles in the tech sector, there has been less focus on how these concerns are actually applied when pressure to deploy increases. This paper introduces the concept of ethics suppression in AI development, highlighting that while ethical oversight may exist on paper, its practical authority can diminish during decision-making. Using a comparative qualitative case study examining corporate governance documents, public statements, and reports on governance issues, we identify common issues such as reduced authority, a weakened ability to escalate concerns, urgency in deployment, and fragmented governance. Our findings indicate that heightened competition can weaken the influence of ethical oversight, even in organisations with established responsible AI practices. By differentiating ethics suppression from ethics washing, it offers a framework for organisations and policymakers to evaluate the effectiveness of ethical oversight in competitive AI development.
articles.author: Victor Frimpong
